newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong assembly approves child deportation bill.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong assembly approves child deportation bill.

text.p: Hong Kong's new legislature has rubber stamped a government bill allowing illegal child immigrants to be deported back to mainland China.

The bill could mean the repatriation of hundreds, possibly thousands, of children who sneaked into Hong Kong to join parents already with residency rights in the former British colony, which became a special Chinese region on July 1.

The new law passed on Wednesday night has kicked up a storm of arguments in the past few days because post-colonial leader Tung Chee-hwa asked the Provisional Legislature to rubber stamp it in a single sitting.
In Hong Kong new bills have traditionally undergone three readings spread over several sessions, but the immigration amendment bill was shoved through in a single day.

Some 60,000 mainland children are said to be awaiting clearance to settle join parents already in Hong Kong, and concessions to those who jumped the queue and were smuggled in illegally could have sparked an influx, the government said.

The Provisional Legislature passed the measure by 45 to six. Human rights groups condemned a backdating of the law to July 1. "Such an abrogation of these children's rights is particularly serious because it sets a precedent...of denying by administrative measures the constitutional rights of the Hong Kong people," Hong Kong Human Rights Monitor said.

But Secretary for Security Peter Lai denied the law was unconstitutional. "The law enacted today does not infringe the right of abode of the mainland children of Hong Kong parents. It only makes them come here in orderly fashion," he said.

The legislature, however, escaped pressure to ram through in similar fashion a law to suspend a string of labour rights bills passed in the last week of colonial rule, after the government eased off and suggested tackling it at next week's sitting.
That legislation has sparked protests from trade unions, pro-democracy legislators and international labour groups, as well as a five day hunger strike by Hong Kong labour leader Lee Cheuk-yan.

Political tenmpers are also flaring over a new election system unveiled by Tung on Tuesday which severely reduces the prospects of pro-democracy candidates winning any seats in the first post-colonial elections next year.

And a legal challenge to the Provisional Legislature's legitimacy is in the offing. A judge on Tuesday set a July 22 hearing for arguments by barristers that Hong Kong had entered a legal vacuum when the handover took place, making laws invalid.

China meanwhile named a new chief negotiator to handle its talks with Britain on implementation of the 1984 treaty under which London handed back its 156-year-old colony, a capitalist bastion of 6.4 million people, mostly Chinese.

Beijing named Wang Guisheng, former director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as its chief representative to the Joint Liaison Group. Wang had his first meeting on Wednesday with Britain's chief diplomat in the group, Hugh Davies.
Wang has been closely involved with Hong Kong and Macau affairs for six years, having worked as counsellor, deputy director and director of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office.
Shouts of "dictatorship" and"rubber stamp" marked the opening of the China-appointed legislature on Wednesday.
Activists from pro-democracy groups demonstrated outside the old colonial legislature building in central Hong Kong in a "day of mourning" for what they called the death of democracy.
